claim: Zebrafish otic vesicle development begins at 12 hours post-fertilization (hpf) with bilateral regions of ectoderm adjacent to the hindbrain proliferating and accumulating to form the otic placodes.
source: Beginning at 12 hpf, bilateral regions of ectoderm adjacent to the hindbrain proliferate and subcutaneously accumulate to form the otic placodes (Figure 1—video 1, Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the developmental timeline of the otic vesicle.

claim: The otic vesicle undergoes mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition between 14-16 hpf.
source: The complex morphology of the inner ear arises from progressive changes in cell number, size, shape, and arrangement along with tissue-level patterns of polarization (12–14 hpf, Figure 1A), mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (14–16 hpf, Figure 1B) and cavitation (16–24 hpf, Figure 1C).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text with reference to specific developmental stages and figures.

claim: Cavitation of the otic vesicle occurs between 16-24 hpf.
source: The complex morphology of the inner ear arises from progressive changes in cell number, size, shape, and arrangement along with tissue-level patterns of polarization (12–14 hpf, Figure 1A), mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (14–16 hpf, Figure 1B) and cavitation (16–24 hpf, Figure 1C).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text with reference to specific developmental stages and figures.

claim: The otic vesicle is a closed ovoid epithelial structure filled with a fluid called endolymph.
source: These steps build a closed ovoid epithelial structure, the otic vesicle, filled with a fluid called endolymph (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the structure of the otic vesicle.

claim: The otic vesicle undergoes rapid growth between 16-45 hpf prior to the development of more complex substructures.
source: After assembly, the otic vesicle undergoes a period of rapid growth (16–45 hpf, Figure 1D) prior to the development of more complex substructures such as the semicircular canals and endolymphatic sac.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the growth timeline of the otic vesicle.

claim: Cell number in the otic vesicle increased nearly three-fold from 415 ± 26 to 1106 ± 52 cells between 16 and 45 hpf.
source: During this period, cell number increased nearly three-fold from 415 ± 26 to 1106 ± 52 cells (blue curve, Figure 1E, for all data-points in Figure 1 n = 10 otic vesicles, data spread is the standard deviation).
evidence: Quantitative data from image analysis presented in the text and Figure 1E.

claim: Average cell size decreased from 0.55 ± 0.02 pl at 16 hpf to 0.34 ± 0.03 pl at 28 hpf and remained constant thereafter.
source: However, cell proliferation was offset by a decrease in average cell size from 0.55 ± 0.02 pl at 16 hpf to 0.34 ± 0.03 pl at 28 hpf and stayed constant thereafter (red curve).
evidence: Quantitative data from image analysis presented in the text and referenced to Figure 1E.

claim: Tissue volume remained effectively constant (230.6 ± 7.4 pl) until 28 hpf and subsequently increased linearly by 132 pl to 45 hpf.
source: Tissue volume, the product of cell number and average cell size, remained effectively constant (230.6 ± 7.4 pl) until 28 hpf and subsequently increased linearly by 132 pl to 45 hpf (green curve, Figure 1F).
evidence: Quantitative data from image analysis presented in the text and Figure 1F.

claim: The volume of the otic vesicle increased dramatically by 572 pl from 235 ± 16 pl to 807 ± 23 pl.
source: The volume of the otic vesicle increased dramatically, by 572 pl from 235 ± 16 pl to 807 ± 23 pl (orange curve).
evidence: Quantitative data from image analysis presented in the text and referenced to Figure 1F.

claim: The majority of the increase in size of the otic vesicle (77%) is due to an increase in lumen volume while tissue growth contributed only 23%.
source: The majority of the increase in size of the otic vesicle is due to an increase in lumen volume (blue curve) from 0 to 440 ± 18 pl (77% of the total increase) while tissue growth contributed only 23% to the increase in size.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of volume data presented in the text and referenced to Figure 1F.

claim: Epithelial thickness of the otic vesicle significantly decreased from 20 µm to 4 µm during otic vesicle growth in lateral and medial regions.
source: Except for the future sensory patches at the anterior and posterior ends (poles), epithelial thickness of the remaining otic vesicle significantly decreased from 20 µm to 4 µm during otic vesicle growth (lateral and medial regions, Figure 1H).
evidence: Quantitative data from image analysis presented in the text and Figure 1H.

claim: Mitotic cells fail to round up fully in regions where the otic epithelium pushes against the hindbrain and ectoderm, in contrast to non-contact regions at the anterioposterior poles.
source: We observed that mitotic cells fail to round up fully in regions where the otic epithelium pushes against the hindbrain and ectoderm, in contrast to non-contact regions at the anterioposterior poles (Figure 2A,C–G).
evidence: Observational data from confocal microscopy presented in the text and Figure 2.

claim: Cell division planes are closely aligned with the surface-normal to the epithelium in contact regions compared to the broader distribution exhibited by non-contact cell populations.
source: Furthermore, cell division planes are closely aligned with the surface-normal to the epithelium (red markers, Figure 2H) in comparison to the broader distribution exhibited by the non-contact cell populations (blue).
evidence: Quantitative data from image analysis presented in the text and Figure 2H.

claim: The overall alignment of cell division planes progressively increases in developmental time as cells become more stretched.
source: The overall alignment progressively increases in developmental time as cells become more stretched (Figure 2I), consistent with mechanical stress driven spindle alignment previously observed in various systems including the zebrafish gastrula (Campinho et al., 2013), fly imaginal disc (Legoff et al., 2013), and zebrafish pre-enveloping layer (Xiong et al., 2014).
evidence: Quantitative data from image analysis presented in the text and Figure 2I, with citation to prior work.

claim: As the vesicle grows, the initially planar hindbrain surface indents in, and the skin bulges out.
source: To test this idea, we quantified the indentation of the hindbrain and otic vesicle interface. We observed that as the vesicle grows, the initially planar hindbrain surface indents in, and the skin bulges out (Figure 2B–F,J).
evidence: Observational and quantitative data from confocal microscopy presented in the text and Figure 2.

claim: Lumenal pressure in the otic vesicle gradually increases from 100 Pa at 30 hpf to upwards of 300 Pa at 48 hpf.
source: We measured the pressure level at 30, 36 and 48 hpf and found that the pressure level gradually increases from 100 Pa to upwards of 300 Pa (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Direct pressure measurements using a novel pressure probe presented in the text and Figure 3C and D.

claim: Pressure measurements in the otic vesicle are similar to prior measurements of the much larger inner ear of adult guinea pigs.
source: These values are similar to prior measurements of the much larger inner ear of adult guinea pigs (Feldman et al., 1979).
evidence: Comparison to prior published measurements cited in the text.

claim: Puncturing the otic vesicle causes an immediate and significant decrease in vesicle diameter and loss of lumenal volume (≈30–40%).
source: Immediately following puncture, we observed a significant decrease in vesicle diameter (white arrows, Figure 3E) and loss of lumenal volume (≈30–40%) (Figure 3F).
evidence: Experimental data from puncture experiments presented in the text and Figure 3E and F.

claim: As the vesicle shrinks after puncture, the epithelium becomes thicker and epithelial cells change shape to become more columnar while preserving cell volume.
source: Examination of punctured vesicles showed that as the vesicle shrunk, the epithelium became thicker (Figure 3E and G). Indeed, the excess surface area of the lumenal cavity was absorbed by a significant change in epithelial cell shape to become more columnar while preserving cell volume (in-plane:normal diameter change from 6.7 ± 0.2 µm:13.2 ± 2.9 µm to 5.9 ± 0.2 µm:18.4 ± 4.1 µm at 30hpf) (Figure 3H).
evidence: Experimental data from puncture experiments presented in the text and Figure 3E, G, and H.

claim: The lumenal fluid is under hydrostatic pressure that is released when the vesicle is punctured.
source: Together, the puncturing experiments provided three insights into the mechanics of the otic vesicle: (i) the lumenal fluid is under hydrostatic pressure that is released when the vesicle is punctured, (ii) lumenal pressure generates stress in the epithelium that alters the shape of epithelial cells, causing them to stretch and become flatter, and (iii) the epithelial tissue response is viscoelastic, being elastic on short time scales, consistent with the epithelium becoming thicker immediately after puncturing, and viscous at longer time scales, consistent with long-term irreversible deformations.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data from puncture experiments presented in the text.

claim: Lumenal pressure generates stress in the epithelium that alters the shape of epithelial cells, causing them to stretch and become flatter.
source: Together, the puncturing experiments provided three insights into the mechanics of the otic vesicle: (i) the lumenal fluid is under hydrostatic pressure that is released when the vesicle is punctured, (ii) lumenal pressure generates stress in the epithelium that alters the shape of epithelial cells, causing them to stretch and become flatter, and (iii) the epithelial tissue response is viscoelastic, being elastic on short time scales, consistent with the epithelium becoming thicker immediately after puncturing, and viscous at longer time scales, consistent with long-term irreversible deformations.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data from puncture experiments presented in the text.

claim: The epithelial tissue response is viscoelastic, being elastic on short time scales and viscous at longer time scales.
source: Together, the puncturing experiments provided three insights into the mechanics of the otic vesicle: (i) the lumenal fluid is under hydrostatic pressure that is released when the vesicle is punctured, (ii) lumenal pressure generates stress in the epithelium that alters the shape of epithelial cells, causing them to stretch and become flatter, and (iii) the epithelial tissue response is viscoelastic, being elastic on short time scales, consistent with the epithelium becoming thicker immediately after puncturing, and viscous at longer time scales, consistent with long-term irreversible deformations.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data from puncture experiments presented in the text.

claim: The vesicle will adjust endolymph flux to account for perturbations to vesicle size, via a mechanical feedback loop that links pressure to flux.
source: Interestingly, analysis of the system of equations in our model shows that the vesicle will adjust endolymph flux to account for perturbations to vesicle size, via a mechanical feedback loop that links pressure to flux (Figure 3J).
evidence: Theoretical prediction from mathematical model presented in the text and Figure 3J.

claim: The otic epithelium rapidly seals after puncture and restores the epithelial barrier within 5 minutes.
source: However, when the dye was injected into the perilymph 5 min after the puncture, there was no rapid movement of dye into the lumen (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D). This showed that the otic epithelium rapidly seals after puncture and restores the epithelial barrier.
evidence: Experimental data from dye injection experiments presented in the text and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Punctured vesicles completely regenerate lumenal volume by an increased growth rate relative to wild type to restore bilateral symmetry.
source: Interestingly, we observed the complete regeneration of lumenal volume in punctured vesicles by an increased growth rate relative to wild type to restore bilateral symmetry (Figure 4B–E, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: Experimental data from puncture and regeneration experiments presented in the text and Figure 4B–E.

claim: Fluid flux in the punctured vesicle correlates with the difference in lumenal volumes between the left and right vesicles.
source: Consistently, fluid flux in the punctured vesicle correlates with the difference in lumenal volumes between the left and right vesicles (blue markers in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for other developmental stages).
evidence: Quantitative data from puncture and regeneration experiments presented in the text and Figure 4H.

claim: Vesicle pressure negatively regulates fluid flux.
source: These data together show that vesicle pressure negatively regulates fluid flux and suggest that this feedback could buffer variations in size and drive catch-up growth in the otic vesicle.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data from puncture and regeneration experiments presented in the text.

claim: Ouabain, an inhibitor of Na+-K+-ATPase pump activity, causes a dose-dependent decrease in otic vesicle volume and wall thickness deformation.
source: We administered ouabain, an inhibitor of Na+-K+-ATPase pump activity, to embryos at the 20 hpf stage and quantified vesicle morphology at 30 hpf. We observed a dose-dependent decrease in otic vesicle volume (blue) and wall thickness deformation (red) compared to the wild-type values (Figure 5A) consistent with previous work (Hoijman et al., 2015).
evidence: Experimental data from drug treatment experiments presented in the text and Figure 5A, with citation to prior work.

claim: Adding 500 µM ouabain to the buffer completely inhibited further growth and post-puncture regeneration in punctured embryos at 25 hpf.
source: In punctured embryos at 25 hpf, adding 500 µM ouabain to the buffer completely inhibited further growth (left vesicle) and post-puncture regeneration (right vesicle in Figure 5B–C, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Experimental data from drug treatment and puncture experiments presented in the text and Figure 5B–C.

claim: Knockdown of Na+-K+-ATPase expression in morpholino-injected embryos inhibited lumenal fluid transport in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Knockdown of Na+-K+-ATPase expression in morpholino-injected embryos inhibited lumenal fluid transport in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5D).
evidence: Experimental data from morpholino knockdown experiments presented in the text and Figure 5D.

claim: Otic vesicle growth is sensitive to variations in extracellular pH and blockers of chloride channel activity.
source: We additionally find that otic vesicle growth is sensitive to variations in extracellular pH and blockers of chloride channel activity (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: Experimental data from pH and drug treatment experiments presented in the text and Figure 5E–F.

claim: The effective viscosity of the otic vesicle tissue is about 6.3 ± 0.30 × 10^6 Pa*s from 24 to 36 hpf and then 2.2 ± 0.13 × 10^7 Pa*s from 36 to 48 hpf.
source: Using this relationship, our morphodynamic measurements, and pressure measurements we estimate the effective viscosity of the otic vesicle tissue to be about 6.3 ± 0.30 × 106 Pa*s from 24 to 36 hpf and then 2.2 ± 0.13 × 107 Pa*s from 36 to 48 hpf (see Materials and methods for error propagation calculations).
evidence: Calculated from quantitative data and mathematical model presented in the text.

claim: The otic vesicle's tissue becomes more viscous through development.
source: These values are within the range of tissue viscosities that had been experimentally measured, (Gordon et al., 1972), and indicate that the otic vesicle's tissue becomes more viscous through development.
evidence: Interpretation of calculated viscosity values presented in the text, with citation to prior work.

claim: Cells retained their columnar shapes independent of the underlying tissue curvature.
source: We found that cells retained their columnar shapes independent of the underlying tissue curvature, suggesting that material property patterning may instead contribute to differential cell strain-rates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Experimental data from cell tracking experiments presented in the text and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Cell stretching has a more significant role in early growth while proliferation plays a more important role in later stages of growth.
source: Thus, we speculated that cell stretching has a more significant role in early growth while proliferation plays a more important role in later stages of growth.
evidence: Interpretation of quantitative data presented in the text.

claim: Lumenal surface area growth is linear through time.
source: Our analysis shows that lumenal surface area growth is linear through time (blue markers).
evidence: Quantitative data from image analysis presented in the text and referenced to Figure 6D.

claim: The contribution from cell-stretching to lumenal surface area growth is high initially but monotonically decreasing and buffered by division.
source: To support this growth, the contribution from cell-stretching is high initially but monotonically decreasing (green markers) and buffered by division (red markers).
evidence: Quantitative data from image analysis presented in the text and referenced to Figure 6D.

claim: A break-even point occurs at around 33 hpf when the contribution to tissue viscosity from cell proliferation exceeds that from cell stretching.
source: A break-even point occurs at around 33 hpf when the contribution to tissue viscosity from cell proliferation exceeds that from cell stretching (dashed black line).
evidence: Quantitative data from image analysis presented in the text and referenced to Figure 6D.

claim: F-actin and Myosin II were apically localized prior to lumenization through 12–16 hpf to form a band around the cavity.
source: Both, F-actin (Figure 6E and Figure 6—video 1) and Myosin II (Figure 6F and Figure 6—video 2) were apically localized prior to lumenization through 12–16 hpf to form a band around the cavity.
evidence: Experimental data from transgenic zebrafish imaging presented in the text and Figure 6E and F.

claim: Through early growth between 16–22 hpf, gradual and non-uniform changes in the apical density of F-actin and Myosin II are observed.
source: Through early growth between 16–22 hpf, gradual and non-uniform changes in the apical density of these molecules are observed.
evidence: Experimental data from transgenic zebrafish imaging presented in the text.

claim: By 30 hpf, F-actin and Myosin II are localized to apicolateral junctions inside cells.
source: By 30 hpf, we find that these proteins are localized to apicolateral junctions inside cells (Figure 6G–H).
evidence: Experimental data from transgenic zebrafish imaging presented in the text and Figure 6G–H.

claim: Wild-type cell deformation during normal growth is positively correlated to localized accumulation of F-actin and Myosin II.
source: We find that wild-type cell deformation during normal growth is positively correlated to localized accumulation of F-actin and Myosin II (Figure 6I).
evidence: Quantitative data from cell tracking experiments presented in the text and Figure 6I.

claim: Upon puncture, the instantaneous deformation observed in individual cells is linearly correlated with the levels of apical localization of F-actin and Myosin II.
source: We find that upon puncture, the instantaneous deformation observed in individual cells is linearly correlated with the levels of apical localization of F-actin and Myosin II suggesting that actomyosin tension sets effective tissue elasticity (Figure 6J).
evidence: Quantitative data from puncture and cell tracking experiments presented in the text and Figure 6J.

claim: Actomyosin tension sets effective tissue elasticity.
source: We find that upon puncture, the instantaneous deformation observed in individual cells is linearly correlated with the levels of apical localization of F-actin and Myosin II suggesting that actomyosin tension sets effective tissue elasticity (Figure 6J).
evidence: Interpretation of quantitative data from puncture and cell tracking experiments presented in the text and Figure 6J.

claim: The decrease in apical myosin fluorescence positively correlated with the increase in secretion rates.
source: The decrease in apical myosin fluorescence positively correlated with the increase in secretion rates (Figure 6L and Figure 6—video 3).
evidence: Quantitative data from drug treatment experiments presented in the text and Figure 6L.

claim: In cytochalasin D treated embryos, the DV diameter was found to increase most, compared to LR and AP diameters that experience reactionary forces from the hindbrain and skin.
source: In these embryos, the DV diameter was found to increase most, compared to LR and AP diameters that experience reactionary forces from the hindbrain and skin (Figure 6M and Figure 6—video 3).
evidence: Quantitative data from drug treatment experiments presented in the text and Figure 6M.

claim: Spatial patterning of the actomyosin cytoskeleton can lead to spatially varied strain in responses to spatially uniform pressure.
source: Together, these data show how spatial patterning of the actomyosin cytokskeleton can lead to spatially varied strain in responses to spatially uniform pressure, and thus contribute to regional differences in the otic vesicle epithelium during growth.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data from drug treatment and imaging experiments presented in the text.

claim: Hydrostatic lumenal pressure develops in the zebrafish otic vesicle in response to fluid transport across the otic epithelium to drive growth.
source: Here, we show that hydrostatic lumenal pressure develops in the zebrafish otic vesicle in response to fluid transport across the otic epithelium to drive growth.
evidence: Summary statement of findings presented in the text.

claim: A hydraulic negative feedback loop exists between pressure and fluid transport for achieving size control in the otic vesicle.
source: With the aid of a multiscale mathematical model, we hypothesized and experimentally confirmed the presence of a hydraulic negative feedback loop between pressure and fluid transport for achieving size control.
evidence: Summary statement of findings presented in the text.

claim: The negative feedback architecture found in the otic vesicle is similar to the chalone model of size control in that the act of growth feeds back to inhibit the rate of growth.
source: The negative feedback architecture that we found is similar to the chalone model of size control in that the act of growth feeds back to inhibit the rate of growth.
evidence: Comparison to existing models presented in the text.

claim: Compared to chalones or morphogen based growth control strategies which are limited in speed by diffusion, the pressure based strategy allows nearly instant communication between different parts of a tissue via hydraulic coupling.
source: However, compared to chalones or morphogen based growth control strategies which are limited in speed by diffusion, the pressure based strategy allows nearly instant communication between different parts of a tissue via hydraulic coupling to allow for 'course corrections' to developmental trajectories.
evidence: Comparison to existing models and interpretation of findings presented in the text.

claim: Sustained cell thinning during otic vesicle development is caused by in-plane epithelial tension in response to lumenal pressure.
source: Here we show that the otic epithelium is fairly elastic and cells can re-thicken following loss of lumenal pressure when the vesicle is punctured (Figure 3G,H), so stretching by neighboring mitotic cells may be short lived. Rather, in our model we postulate that sustained cell thinning during otic vesicle development is caused by in-plane epithelial tension in response to lumenal pressure.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data and model predictions presented in the text.

claim: Transepithelial fluid flow is the primary if not sole source of fluid accumulation in the lumen.
source: Further, our measurements show that the lumen volume continues to grow until it exceeds the tissue volume (Figure 1F). We thus infer that transepithelial fluid flow is the primary if not sole source of fluid accumulation in the lumen.
evidence: Interpretation of quantitative data presented in the text and Figure 1F.

claim: Fluid pressure is a fundamental regulator of developmental growth in lumenized organs.
source: Here we use a newly revealed instance of catch-up growth combined with physical theory to uncover how size control is achieved in the zebrafish otic vesicle, a fluid-filled closed epithelium that develops into the inner ear. We postulate that fluid pressure is a fundamental regulator of developmental growth in lumenized organs and hydraulic feedback can give rise to robust control of size.
evidence: Summary statement of findings and postulate presented in the text.

claim: Hydraulic feedback can give rise to robust control of size in lumenized organs.
source: Here we use a newly revealed instance of catch-up growth combined with physical theory to uncover how size control is achieved in the zebrafish otic vesicle, a fluid-filled closed epithelium that develops into the inner ear. We postulate that fluid pressure is a fundamental regulator of developmental growth in lumenized organs and hydraulic feedback can give rise to robust control of size.
evidence: Summary statement of findings and postulate presented in the text.

claim: Hydraulic interactions are relevant to the developmental growth of many internal organs with vesicular and tubular origins.
source: Indeed, our study is in line with the fact that hydraulic interactions are relevant to the developmental growth of many internal organs with vesicular and tubular origins (Ruiz-Herrero et al., 2017), and most recently the entire mammalian embryo (Chan et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement connecting findings to broader context with citations to prior work.

claim: Pressure homeostasis mechanisms may vary across different organs and developmental stages.
source: Pressure homeostasis mechanisms may vary. In the inner ear, pressure is initially regulated by feedback between pressure and lumenal fluid flux. However later in development, we have found that a physical pressure relief valve is necessary for pressure homeostasis in the inner ear (Swinburne et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement of findings with citation to prior work.

claim: In the inner ear, pressure is initially regulated by feedback between pressure and lumenal fluid flux.
source: Pressure homeostasis mechanisms may vary. In the inner ear, pressure is initially regulated by feedback between pressure and lumenal fluid flux. However later in development, we have found that a physical pressure relief valve is necessary for pressure homeostasis in the inner ear (Swinburne et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement of findings presented in the text.

claim: Later in development, a physical pressure relief valve is necessary for pressure homeostasis in the inner ear.
source: Pressure homeostasis mechanisms may vary. In the inner ear, pressure is initially regulated by feedback between pressure and lumenal fluid flux. However later in development, we have found that a physical pressure relief valve is necessary for pressure homeostasis in the inner ear (Swinburne et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement of findings with citation to prior work.

claim: Fluid accumulation is a feature of developmental growth for several luminized organs including the embryonic brain, eye, gut, Kupffer's vesicle, the inner ear, and the whole mammalian embryo.
source: In particular, fluid accumulation is a feature of developmental growth for several luminized organs including the embryonic brain (Desmond and Jacobson, 1977; Lowery and Sive, 2005), eye (Coulombre, 1956), gut (Bagnat et al., 2007), Kupffer's vesicle (Navis et al., 2013; Dasgupta et al., 2018), the inner ear (Abbas and Whitfield, 2009; Hoijman et al., 2015), and the whole mammalian embryo (Chan et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: Water transport across an epithelium underlies the phenomenon of fluid accumulation in luminized organs.
source: Water transport across an epithelium underlies these phenomenon (Frömter and Diamond, 1972; Günzel and Yu, 2013; Rubashkin et al., 2006; Fischbarg, 2010), and for the developing brain and eye it was shown that fluid accumulation coincides with increased hydrostatic pressure (Desmond and Jacobson, 1977; Coulombre, 1956).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: For the developing brain and eye, fluid accumulation coincides with increased hydrostatic pressure.
source: Water transport across an epithelium underlies these phenomenon (Frömter and Diamond, 1972; Günzel and Yu, 2013; Rubashkin et al., 2006; Fischbarg, 2010), and for the developing brain and eye it was shown that fluid accumulation coincides with increased hydrostatic pressure (Desmond and Jacobson, 1977; Coulombre, 1956).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: Specific ion transporters necessary for fluid accumulation have been identified in various organs.
source: Although specific ion transporters necessary for fluid accumulation have been identified (Lowery and Sive, 2005; Bagnat et al., 2007; Navis et al., 2013; Abbas and Whitfield, 2009), it is only very recently that we are beginning to get a glimpse of how how ion transport and transepithelial fluid flow are regulated, and their role in growth control, and much still remains to be explored .
evidence: Statement of established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: Catch-up growth during development is the phenomenon where, after growth delay or perturbation, an organ transiently elevates its growth rate relative to other organs to get back on course.
source: Catch-up growth during development is the phenomenon where, after growth delay or perturbation, an organ transiently elevates its growth rate relative to other organs to get back on course.
evidence: Definition of catch-up growth presented in the text.

claim: During fly development, if the growth of one imaginal disc is perturbed then a hormone, ecdysone, signals to the other imaginal discs to slow their growth such that the perturbed organ can catch-up and the animal's coordinated growth can resume.
source: During fly development, if the growth of one imaginal disc is perturbed then a hormone, ecdysone, signals to the other imaginal discs to slow their growth such that the perturbed organ can catch-up and the animal's coordinated growth can resume (Parker and Shingleton, 2011).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge with citation to prior work.

claim: If an infant heart or kidney is transplanted into an adult, it grows faster than the surrounding tissue to catch-up to a target size.
source: Catch-up growth also occurs in vertebrates: if an infant heart or kidney is transplanted into an adult, it grows faster than the surrounding tissue to catch-up to a target size (Dittmer et al., 1974; Silber, 1976).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: The study of catch-up growth during bone growth has clarified insulin signaling activity as being important for bone size control.
source: Catch-up growth also occurs during bone growth and its study has clarified insulin signaling activity as being important for bone size control (Roselló-Díez and Joyner, 2015; Roselló-Díez et al., 2017; Roselló-Díez et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: Dysregulation of pressure homeostasis can give rise to diseases including hypertension in the vasculature, Ménière's disease in the inner ear, glaucoma in the eye, and hydrocephalus in the brain.
source: Dysregulation of pressure homeostasis can give rise to diseases including hypertension in the vasculature, Ménière's disease in the inner ear, glaucoma in the eye, and hydrocephalus in the brain.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge presented in the text.

claim: The otic vesicle is wedged between the hindbrain and skin.
source: Given that the otic vesicle is wedged between the hindbrain and skin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–H), we examined the impact of its volumetric growth on these tissues.
evidence: Observational data from imaging presented in the text and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–H.

claim: The otic vesicle is not growing in isolation but is immediately surrounded by extracellular matrix, mesenchymal cells, skin, and the brain.
source: The otic vesicle is not growing in isolation. In the embryo, it is immediately surrounded by extracellular matrix, mesenchymal cells, skin, and the brain.
evidence: Statement of observational context presented in the text.

claim: Prior work in the chick otic vesicle identified the activity of Na+-K+-ATPase in setting up a transmural potential to drive the selective movement of water and ions.
source: Previous work in the chick otic vesicle identified the activity of Na+-K+-ATPase in setting up a transmural potential (Represa et al., 1986) to drive the selective movement of water and ions.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge with citation to prior work.

claim: In the zebrafish, a role for ion pumps in ear growth is supported by the previous identification of the Na+-K+-Cl− transporter Slc12a2 as defective in little ear mutants.
source: In the zebrafish, a role for ion pumps in ear growth is supported by the previous identification of the Na+-K+-Cl− transporter Slc12a2 as defective in little ear mutants (Abbas and Whitfield, 2009).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge with citation to prior work.
